title: Terracotta statuette of a horse

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Purchase, Abraham Foundation Gift, 2000
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A small clay statuette of a horse, made in a Greek city in southern Italy. The sculpted animal has a horse's long neck, head, and sturdy body.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, culture, date, medium, classification, tags (Horses), public-domain flag, credit line, and image URLs read from the record

context: A small terracotta horse made in the Greek-speaking world of southern Italy, in the area of Taras (modern Taranto), around the 4th to 3rd century BCE. Such figurines were made in molds and by hand, and are often found in graves and sanctuaries.

descriptions.k: This is a little horse made of clay. It was made long ago in a Greek city in Italy. Can you see its long neck and strong body? How do you think a horse like this would move?
descriptions.g12: A clay horse from a Greek town in southern Italy, made over 2,000 years ago. It is small enough to hold. Look at the long neck, the head, and the strong body. The artist shaped each part to make it look like a real horse. What would you name this horse?
descriptions.g35: This small clay horse comes from the Greek city of Taras in southern Italy, which is now called Taranto. Horses were important to the Greeks, who used them for travel, farming, and games. An artist shaped the clay by hand or pressed it into a mold, then baked it hard. Look for the shapes that make it a horse. Why might someone have made, owned, or given a clay horse?
descriptions.g68: Terracotta, or baked clay, was a common material for small sculptures in the Greek world, and Taras was known for making them. This horse is dated to the 4th–3rd century BCE. Horses stood for speed, strength, and wealth in Greek culture, and small figures may have been offered in sanctuaries or placed in graves, though the use of any single piece is uncertain. Look closely at how the artist simplifies the animal's anatomy. Which parts get the most attention?
descriptions.g910: A terracotta horse from the Greek cities of southern Italy shows how Greek visual culture spread beyond Greece itself. Horses carried associations of status, athletics, and nobility, and a small clay version made them available to many more people than a bronze or marble statue. Consider how the maker simplifies anatomy while keeping a convincing sense of the animal's weight and alertness. What choices matter most when a living animal is translated into a small baked-clay form?
descriptions.g1112: This statuette belongs to a broad tradition of terracotta production in the Greek West, where Taras was a significant center. Scholars link such figurines to votive offerings, burials, and domestic settings, but a specific find context matters and is not given here, so any claim about its purpose is provisional. Formally, the piece offers a case study in how a modest medium translates naturalistic observation into a compact form. It also invites reflection on how we value small, often anonymous, works compared with celebrated monumental sculpture.

teacherNote.context: A terracotta horse of the 4th–3rd century BCE from the Greek-speaking world of southern Italy, labeled Tarentine in the Met record. Small clay figures were widespread in Greek communities.
directions: Have students model a small animal from clay or playdough, then discuss what they simplified.
Locate southern Italy and Greece on a map and discuss how Greek settlers carried culture overseas.
Compare the clay horse with a photograph of a real horse and note what the artist kept and left out.
